query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled low-temperature annealing of the metastable Mg-containing HEA will cause diffusion‐activated nucleation of finely dispersed Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds that mediate partitioning of Ti and Zn to grain boundaries, thereby promoting the formation of a uniform TiO2/ZnO passivating film and retaining corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight HEA in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state (similar to compositions studied in PMC10728166 and PMC11330973).
generation.intervention: Isothermal annealing at a moderate temperature (e.g., ~350°C) for controlled durations (e.g., 1–5 hours).
generation.conditions: Ambient pressure annealing in an inert atmosphere followed by exposure to simulated service environment (e.g., NaCl solution for corrosion and 600°C oxidative atmosphere), within service regime boundaries below 500°C for prolonged exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine, uniformly dispersed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates and grain boundary segregation of Ti/Zn.
generation.mechanism: Diffusional activation leads to controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallics, which sequester and redistribute key alloying elements (Ti and Zn) to form, upon high-temperature exposure, a continuous and protective oxide film.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed at ~350°C will exhibit a modest intermetallic volume fraction (estimated <20%) with enhanced formation of homogeneous passivating oxides, resulting in 20–30% improvement in corrosion current density and reduced oxidation kinetics compared to the as-quenched baseline.
generation.baseline: The initial metastable solid solution produced by rapid cooling exhibits lower corrosion and oxidation resistance upon subsequent service exposure due to uncontrolled intermetallic formation.
generation.boundary: Service-regime temperatures maintained below ~500°C and exposure times within the accelerated test window (e.g., up to 100 hours) to avoid extensive coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature and time thresholds for optimal intermetallic size and distribution may vary with composition nuances; diffusion rates in complex alloys may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one rapidly quenched (maintaining metastable state) and one annealed at ~350°C. Characterize intermetallic volume fraction with TEM/XRD, measure corrosion performance in NaCl solution using potentiodynamic polarization, and assess oxidation layer formation after high-temperature exposure.
measurements: TEM and XRD for intermetallic phase identification and volume fraction
XPS/SEM for oxide film morphology and composition
High-temperature oxidation kinetics via thermogravimetric analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a significant (e.g., >20%) improvement in corrosion/oxidation resistance in conjunction with a moderate (finely dispersed) intermetallic fraction compared to the rapid quench baseline, then the mechanism of intermetallic-mediated element partitioning leading to improved passivation is falsified.

This brings up an important question: How stable are the identified topmost compositions (with the lowest formation energy) in SS state against their compound phases at room temperature? To answer the question, we used the Grand Canonical Linear Programming (GCLP) method developed by Wolverton et al. for metallic compounds. The method maps a free energy minimization problem to a linear algebra problem to predict the free energy minimum for a given composition at room temperature. We compared the formation energy for the most stable HEA compositions obtained at T = 0 K and room temperature (T = 300 K). cited_evidence.text: Our results indicated that kinetics of phase transformation plays a crucial role in phase selection of the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA. The phases can be controlled using kinetic ways according to the CCT curve. It seems that the sluggish diffusion in HEAs did not affect the kinetic behavior in this alloy system especially in the intermediate temperature. In fact, kinetic effect not only works for the special CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA but affects the phase selection of all HEAs. Li et al. reported that BCC phase can be obtained by supercooling method in the well-known FCC single phase CoCrFeNi HEA and the mechanical properties of the HEA was enhanced by three times. The rapid solidification behavior of CoCrCuNiFex HEA was also studied and useful nano-phases were found in the matrix, which would unquestionably strengthen the HEA dramatically. Ravi et al. reported that synthesis route can have a significant influence on the process of phase-choice and -evolution in different HEAs and this is actually a result of kinetic effect. The selected Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 and Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8 alloys were analysed for structural behavior by CALPHAD, solidification and kinetics simulations. Phase diagrams showed the formation of a multiphase structure with preponderant solid solutions. Intermetallic compound-based phases were found at lower concentrations but still significantly higher than in the conventional aluminum alloys. Two invariant transformations were indicated for Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, with a BCC-A2 phase stable between 316–488 °C. The influence of the elements on the structural evolution were similar with the results obtained from semiempirical criteria calculations. The non-equilibrium solidification simulation discussed the order of which the phases are solidifying in normal casting conditions. papers.title: First principles-based design of lightweight high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Lightweight HEAs based on quinary systems such as AlBeMgTiSi, AlBeMgTiCu, and AlBeMgTiLi.
papers.approach: Density functional theory calculations at 0 K combined with the Grand Canonical Linear Programming method (including configurational entropy at 300 K) to gauge formation energies.
papers.findings: Only the AlBeMgTiSi composition is predicted to be energetically stable in a single solid‐solution state at room temperature; the others (AlBeMgTiCu and AlBeMgTiLi) are metastable and prone to compound segregation unless rapid cooling is used.
papers.mechanism: Thermodynamic driving force versus configurational entropy stabilization governs whether a metastable solid‐solution remains intact or transforms via intermetallic compound nucleation.

papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Results of Selected Lightweight Complex Concentrated Alloys, before and after Heat Treatment.
papers.system: Al-Cu/Si-Zn-Mg alloys including systems like Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 and Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8.
papers.approach: CALPHAD-based phase diagram calculations, detailed solidification and diffusion-driven precipitation kinetics simulations, alongside experimental heat treatment and microstructural characterization.
papers.findings: Initial as-cast microstructures composed mainly of solid solutions transform during heat treatment to include significant amounts of intermetallic compound phases (e.g., Mg2Si, Al2Cu) with distinct invariant transformations; the pathway and volume fraction of these IMCs depend on alloy composition and processing history.
papers.mechanism: Diffusional processes during solidification and subsequent annealing drive the nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases from an initially metastable solid solution.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of MgTiZn and Mg₄TiZn Alloys After Ball Milling and Subsequent Spark Plasma Sintering.
papers.system: Mg-Ti-Zn alloys processed via high-energy ball milling and spark plasma sintering; two compositions (equimolar MgTiZn and Mg₄TiZn) were studied.
papers.approach: Powder metallurgy route combining ball milling and SPS, with microstructural analysis (XRD, STEM, XPS) and electrochemical corrosion testing in NaCl solution.
papers.findings: The metastable microstructure in the ball milled/SPS alloys reveals differences: one alloy (TZ) shows abundant fine intermetallic phases and a passivating TiO₂-rich surface film that confer high corrosion resistance, while the other (4TZ) exhibits a more homogeneous Mg-rich solid solution; these differences correlate with the processing-induced microstructural evolution.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between the nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds and the formation of protective oxide/passivating surface films (involving Ti and Zn) governs the retention or loss of corrosion resistance.

papers.title: Kinetic ways of tailoring phases in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiTi₀.₄ HEA (with implications for analogous Mg-containing systems).
papers.approach: Systematic control of cooling rates during solidification and post-solidification annealing, with analysis via transformation kinetics (CCT curves) and phase identification.
papers.findings: Cooling rate strongly influences phase formation—in extremely rapid cooling, nonequilibrium phases (supersaturated FCC and Laves) are retained, while slower cooling enables the transformation into equilibrium intermetallic compounds (σ, γ′, R phases).
papers.mechanism: Kinetic control, via differing cooling rates and diffusion limitations, determines if the metastable solid solution remains or if intermetallic phases nucleate and grow; this effect can be used to design desired phase fractions.

papers.title: Lightweight single-phase Al-based complex concentrated alloy with high specific strength.
papers.system: Al55Mg35Li5Zn5 complex concentrated alloy (CCA) containing Mg; processed under high-pressure, high-temperature conditions to achieve a metastable single-phase FCC microstructure.
papers.approach: High-pressure high-temperature synthesis guided by synchrotron XRD and microstructural analyses, focused on correlating phase stability with mechanical and oxidation performance.
papers.findings: The formation of a metastable single-phase FCC solid solution is enabled by applying both high temperature (for sufficient atomic diffusion) and high pressure (to suppress intermetallic compound formation), resulting in superior mechanical properties and potential for high-temperature oxidation resistance.
papers.mechanism: Enhanced configurational entropy and mitigated atomic size mismatch under HPHT conditions stabilize the metastable state, with the interplay of atomic diffusion and elemental partitioning influencing the emergence of intermetallics if the kinetic window is not maintained.

established: Mg-containing lightweight HEAs can be prepared in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution state by rapid processing methods (ball milling, SPS, rapid cooling, HPHT) as shown by first principles and experimental studies.
Intermetallic compounds readily form from metastable solid solutions during subsequent heat treatments, driven by diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth processes.

The microstructural evolution, including the distribution and morphology of intermetallic phases, strongly influences corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance, often through the formation of passivating oxide films (e.g., TiO₂, Al₂O₃).

approaches_tried.approach: First principles-based thermodynamic calculations with added configurational entropy
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified compositions that are stable versus those that are metastable and prone to compound segregation.

approaches_tried.approach: CALPHAD and kinetics simulations along with experimental heat treatments
approaches_tried.outcome: Detailed mapping of phase transformation pathways and the formation of various intermetallics under different thermal regimes.

approaches_tried.approach: Powder metallurgy using ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS)
approaches_tried.outcome: Engineered metastable microstructures in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys with variable intermetallic phase content and associated differences in corrosion resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Kinetic control of cooling rates during solidification and annealing
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated the suppression or promotion of intermetallic compound formation by tuning the processing kinetics.

mechanisms: Diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from an initially metastable solid solution.
Kinetic hindrance (via rapid cooling, high-pressure/temperature conditions) that can retain a supersaturated solid solution state, preventing or delaying phase separation.

Formation of protective oxide/passivation layers influenced by the spatial distribution of intermetallic phases and residual solid solution, which in turn affects corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
disagreements: Whether high-pressure and high-temperature processing can completely suppress intermetallic formation versus merely delaying transformation kinetics.
The extent to which kinetic arrest (via rapid processing) can maintain corrosion-resistant microstructures compared to the inevitable diffusion-driven phase separation during service conditions.
open_questions: What are the specific kinetic parameters (e.g., diffusion rates, nucleation barriers) governing the transformation from metastable solid solution to intermetallic compounds in Mg-containing HEAs under service regime temperatures?
How does the evolution of intermetallic phases quantitatively correlate with the loss or retention of corrosion and oxidation resistance over long-term exposure?
Under what controlled processing and service conditions will the metastable state be robust enough to preserve the desired passivating surface films?
opportunities: A controlled comparison between samples maintained in a rapid-cooled/metastable state versus those subjected to a deliberate, moderate anneal to trigger intermetallic precipitation could isolate the kinetic effects.
In situ high-temperature and corrosion testing (e.g., using TEM and electrochemical cells) to directly observe phase evolution and oxide/passivation film formation under service-relevant conditions.

Combining high-pressure/temperature processing with varied cooling rates to map out the transformation kinetics, aiming to design alloys where the metastable state is maintained within the targeted service-regime boundaries.

Further studies to quantify the rate of intermetallic nucleation versus passivating film stability, establishing clear falsification criteria: if altering the kinetic conditions does not change the corrosion/oxidation performance or microstructural evolution, then the proposed kinetic mechanism may be invalid.

directions.direction: Investigate thermally activated, diffusion‐controlled nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from the metastable solid solution.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the transformation pathway by linking kinetic parameters (temperature and time) to the onset and morphology of intermetallics; well supported by CALPHAD and kinetic studies (e.g., PMC7579168, PMC5043342) and is experimentally feasible.

directions.direction: Examine the role of intermetallic spatial distribution in mediating the formation and stability of surface passivating oxide films (e.g., TiO2 and ZnO).
directions.assessment: Connects microstructural evolution to corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance by focusing on how uniform or inhomogeneous dispersions can promote or hinder passivation; supported by studies on Mg-Ti-Zn alloys (e.g., PMC12299034) and oxidation mechanisms (e.g., PMC9026100).

directions.direction: Assess the impact of a high-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) processing route on delaying or controlling intermetallic compound formation under subsequent service conditions.
directions.assessment: Builds on evidence that HPHT conditions can stabilize metastable phases (PMC11330973) and modulate the diffusion kinetics, providing a controlled initial state whose transformation kinetics can be finely tuned; addresses service regime boundaries directly.

directions.direction: Implement a controlled annealing study comparing rapidly quenched versus moderately annealed samples to delineate kinetic windows for intermetallic formation and the subsequent effect on passivating film stability.
directions.assessment: Allows the isolation of transformation kinetics, enabling a controlled comparison between samples; supported by diffraction and in situ kinetics work in HEAs (e.g., PMC5043342, PMC7579168); creates a clear falsification possibility if corrosion/oxidation performance does not correlate with intermetallic evolution.

directions.direction: Develop diffusional modeling and simulation of the transformation pathway in Mg-containing HEAs to predict the intermetallic volume fraction evolution and its impact on local chemistry and passivation.
directions.assessment: Offers quantitative insights into the diffusion coefficients and nucleation barriers but is less immediately direct in providing mechanistic insight without complementary experiments; useful for guiding experiments, yet with higher uncertainty in complex multi‐component systems.

candidates.hypothesis: Controlled low-temperature annealing of the metastable Mg-containing HEA will cause diffusion‐activated nucleation of finely dispersed Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds that mediate partitioning of Ti and Zn to grain boundaries, thereby promoting the formation of a uniform TiO2/ZnO passivating film and retaining corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
candidates.intervention: Isothermal annealing at a moderate temperature (e.g., ~350°C) for controlled durations (e.g., 1–5 hours).

candidates.hypothesis: Enhancing surface passivation by engineering a uniformly distributed, fine intermetallic dispersion at grain boundaries will result in preferential segregation of Ti and Zn, which upon high-temperature service forms a stable, continuous TiO2-rich oxide film that significantly reduces oxidation rate.
candidates.intervention: A surface-modification annealing treatment (e.g., a two-step thermal protocol with a short pre-anneal at 350°C followed by a rapid cooling step) aimed at promoting uniform intermetallic nucleation at grain boundaries.

candidates.hypothesis: Mg-containing HEAs processed via HPHT that initially retain their metastable single-phase solid solution will, under controlled moderate annealing (e.g., 400°C), undergo a limited, kinetically controlled transformation to form a low volume fraction (<20%) of nanoscale intermetallic compounds that do not disrupt but actually enhance the formation of protective oxide films during service.
candidates.intervention: Subject the HPHT-synthesized alloy to a moderate isothermal anneal at ~400°C for varying durations (1–4 hours) to trigger partial transformation.

candidates.hypothesis: A direct controlled comparison between rapidly quenched (metastable) and moderately annealed Mg-containing HEAs will reveal that the kinetics of intermetallic compound formation critically determine the integrity of passivating surface films; specifically, premature coarsening of intermetallics beyond an optimal threshold (e.g., >30% volume fraction) will disrupt the continuity of the passivation layer, thereby reducing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
candidates.intervention: Apply two post-processing heat treatments: (a) rapid quench to maintain metastability and (b) deliberate moderate annealing aimed at inducing intermetallic formation to varying extents.

major_issues: Does not clarify how magnesium’s role in the metastable-to-stable transformation pathway contributes to passivation, placing more emphasis on Ti/Zn without showing why Mg is comparatively unimportant.
Details about how the non-equilibrium initial state specifically evolves into the proposed intermetallic distribution are not sufficiently explained.
minor_issues: Unclear rationale for why a two-step thermal protocol at 350°C is optimal, as time/temperature windows are not fully justified.
Extrapolation of a 25% improvement in oxidation resistance is stated but not substantiated with prior data for Mg-containing alloys.
fixes: Elaborate on Mg’s part in the passivation and intermetallic formation processes, explaining how it interacts with Ti/Zn segregation at grain boundaries.
Provide mechanistic details about how the metastable solid solution is expected to evolve into the uniform intermetallic dispersion under the stated thermal profile.
Justify the specific selection of annealing parameters (temperature, duration) with reference to known diffusion data or prior studies.
evidence_needs: Quantitative data or precedent showing that Ti/Zn segregation alone can dominate passivation in a Mg-rich environment.
Experimental or computational demonstrations of how intermetallics affect oxide film formation in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys, especially under high-temperature conditions.

major_issues: Reliance on a specific 30% intermetallic volume fraction threshold is not thoroughly justified and may oversimplify the complex microstructural evolution in Mg-containing HEAs.

fixes: Provide a rationale (theoretical or experimental) for the 30% intermetallic volume fraction limit proposed as critical for passivation.

fixes: Offer more data or references clarifying how the moderate annealing temperature was chosen to achieve partial intermetallic precipitation without excessive coarsening.
